title: About Tetanus

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Tetanus is an infection caused by bacteria called Clostridium tetani (C. tetani), that are found in the environment. Tetanus is an uncommon but very serious disease that requires immediate treatment in a hospital.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Symptoms typically occur between 3 and 21 days (average 8 days) after someone is exposed to C. tetani.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: The first sign is most commonly spasms of the jaw muscles, or "lockjaw."

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Other symptoms can include:

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Trouble swallowing

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Sudden, involuntary muscle spasms — often in the stomach

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Painful muscle stiffness all over the body

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Seizures (jerking or staring)

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Headache

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Fever and sweating

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Changes in blood pressure and heart rate

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Tetanus can cause serious health problems, including:

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Laryngospasm (uncontrolled tightening of the vocal cords)

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Fracture (broken bone)

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Pulmonary embolism (blockage in lungs caused by a blood clot)

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Aspiration pneumonia (lung infection from inhaling spit or vomit)

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Breathing difficulty

sections.heading: Complications
sections.text: Tetanus can lead to death (1 in 10 cases in the United States are fatal).

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Anyone can get tetanus. However, several factors increase the risk for tetanus infection.

sections.heading: Vaccination status
sections.text: People who have never received a tetanus vaccine are at increased risk. Similarly, people who did not complete the primary series or who aren't up to date with their 10-year tetanus booster shots are also at increased risk.

sections.heading: Recent wound
sections.text: People with a recent wound are at increased risk for tetanus. This is especially true if the wound is deep or contaminated with dirt.

sections.heading: Other risk factors
sections.text: The following risk factors are also associated with an increased risk of tetanus:

sections.heading: Other risk factors
sections.text: Being 80 years or older

sections.heading: Other risk factors
sections.text: Having diabetes

sections.heading: Other risk factors
sections.text: Having an immunocompromising condition

sections.heading: Other risk factors
sections.text: Using injection drugs

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: Tetanus bacteria can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries.

sections.heading: Vaccination is the best way to protect against tetanus
sections.text: CDC recommends tetanus vaccination for everyone. The best way to prevent tetanus is to make sure you are up to date on your vaccination.

sections.heading: Care for wounds to prevent infection
sections.text: Immediate and good wound care can help prevent infection.

sections.heading: Care for wounds to prevent infection
sections.text: Apply first aid to even minor, non-infected wounds

sections.heading: Care for wounds to prevent infection
sections.text: Wash hands with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand rub

sections.heading: Care for wounds to prevent infection
sections.text: Consult a healthcare provider if you have concerns or if the wounds: Are from a puncture wound or are deep (e.g., stepping on a nail) Contain dirt, soil, feces, or saliva (e.g., animal bite) Contain dead tissue including from burns, fractures, crush injuries, or frostbite

sections.heading: Medicine and a tetanus vaccination may be needed after some wounds to prevent infection
sections.text: Medicine called human tetanus immune globulin (TIG) can help prevent tetanus. Healthcare providers can use it when someone is not up to date with tetanus vaccination and has serious or contaminated wounds. Vaccination also helps prevent tetanus in people with wounds, depending on their tetanus vaccination history.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text: Healthcare providers usually decide if someone has tetanus by looking for common signs and symptoms. They may also ask about a recent history of cuts, scrapes, punctures, and trauma.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text: No lab or other kinds of tests can confirm tetanus.

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Tetanus is a medical emergency requiring:

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Evaluation and care in the hospital

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Immediate treatment with TIG

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Aggressive wound care

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Drugs to control muscle spasms

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Antibiotics

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Tetanus vaccination

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: Depending on how serious the infection is, someone with tetanus may need a machine to help them breathe.

CDC recommends tetanus vaccination for everyone. The best way to prevent tetanus is to make sure you are up to date on your vaccination.
